Shares of technology giant Apple (AAPL) had an interesting first calendar month of 2018. The stock dropped in February as guidance was short of expectations, helped by a huge pullback in the overall market. Concerns over iPhone sales built throughout the period, which may explain this piece I recently read in a Bloomberg article:
Institutional investors havent been this skeptical on Apple Inc. since at least the financial crisis. They reduced their holdings in the iPhone maker by about 153 million shares in the first three months of the year, an analysis of 13F filings showed. Thats the biggest decrease since at least the first quarter of 2008 when Bloomberg started tracking the data. Its also the most among any S&P 500 stock in the first quarter.
Reading through the article would give you a very bearish view of Apple, which seemed to be in-line with the street’s thinking during the period. Since then, fears have been calmed by management, and shares have risen to new all-time highs. But if the words above didn’t prove negative enough for you, Bloomberg’s article also contained the following image.
(Source: Bloomberg article linked above)
Now I found it interesting that the article did not contain one of two key words: Buyback or repurchase. Why do I say that? Well, Apple management repurchased a massive amount of shares during the quarter, reducing the outstanding count by nearly 140 million in the period. When a company reduces its outstanding share number by that much in a single quarter, it’s a significant number of shares less for investors to own.
In fact, Bloomberg shows how institutional investors have been selling Apple shares quite a bit in the past four calendar quarters. Well, the company has been buying back shares for years now, reducing the outstanding count from over 6.5 billion to under 5 billion. It’s simple math that tells us that there just aren’t as many shares available to own. The following chart shows how much the situation had changed even before the nearly 140 million share count reduction in fiscal Q2 2018.
(Source: Apple 10-Q filings page)
Apple management has detailed its plans to go to a cash neutral situation, which means several billion dollars more per quarter in buybacks moving forward. That means that the outstanding share count will continue to come down for an indefinite time period, likely to 4.5 billion in the next year or two and then possibly 4.0 billion or less in the years following. That likely means we’ll see more institutional selling over time, as there will be less shares overall to own.
In the end, the Bloomberg article talking about massive institutional selling in Apple is misleading at best. While it may be true that the most shares in a quarter were sold since 2008, it doesn’t necessarily mean the street is the most bearish about the name since the financial crisis. Overall, Apple is reducing its share count significantly, which likely has a natural selling impact on institutional holdings. If the street was so bearish, more than 50 million shares would be short currently. However, that number is just a very small fraction of the 291 million shares short (adjusting for the split) that were short Apple back in April 2013, telling you that there aren’t a ton of bets against the name right now.
